editions.title: Tariffs on 14-16 trading partners as AI rout and Nvidia curbs rattle markets
editions.notification: US unveils tariffs of up to 20% on 16 trading partners, and Nvidia reportedly pauses chip shipments to four Asian states.
editions.intro:
The biggest story of the day is the United States' move to impose new Section 301 tariffs on at least 14, and by some accounts 16, trading partners, including China, the EU, Japan, Vietnam, India and Bangladesh. Duties could reach 20%, with rates varying by the trade deals each country has struck. The measures follow the Supreme Court's February ruling against Trump's earlier tariffs and are based on alleged excess manufacturing capacity. China has warned it reserves the right to retaliate, and the fragile US-China trade truce is now under strain. Hong Kong's market fell on the news, and footwear makers warn the costs will fall on American consumers.

The tech sector is also in focus. Reports say Nvidia has halted chip and server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia while it reviews whether partners meet US export rules, a move that could disrupt server supply chains. Separately, Blackwell servers banned from China were reportedly found in a Shanghai data centre linked to Megaspeed, a firm recently blacklisted by Washington. Nvidia has been reinstated under Jensen Huang, but governance probes and a rating warning from S&P keep it under pressure. Anthropic's shares recovered to about $92 after a volatile week, and US indices posted their best weekly gains in a long time, though analysts say the Nvidia probes and AI profitability questions remain unresolved.

Elsewhere, the Gulf conflict is widening: an Iranian-linked drone strike in Kuwait killed two Italian workers, which Iran denies, and Houthi attacks are battering Saudi Arabia's economy. Brent crude rose towards $98. In Europe, Spain votes on Sunday in a close election, EU leaders failed to agree the 2028-34 budget, and S&P moved France's outlook to negative. In Britain, the DWP's online services were taken offline after a cyber incident, though benefit payments continue.

editions.notification: Nvidia's Huang is reinstated, yet the AI sell-off resumes and S&P puts Nvidia on downgrade watch.
editions.intro:
Nvidia dominated the day again, a week after Jensen Huang's resignation and reinstatement. The shares, which surged more than 30% when he returned, have since slid back. On Wednesday S&P Global Ratings put the company's AA rating on watch for a possible downgrade, citing board governance, and four congressional committees and several probes still want answers. Reports also say Nvidia has paused chip and server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia as US export licensing tightens. The company's troubles are feeding a wider AI sell-off that has pushed US indices into correction and drained foreign money from Taiwan.

Trade and geopolitics were the other big stories. Washington has moved to impose Section 301 tariffs on at least 14 trading partners, with rates of up to 20 per cent depending on each country's deal, though implementation is not expected before late February or March. In the Gulf, Houthi strikes on Saudi energy sites and a fatal drone incident in Kuwait that Iran calls a set-up have pushed Brent back near $96 a barrel. In Britain, Prime Minister Andy Burnham's EU reset deals drew fresh scrutiny, including a 4% participation fee, while Altria's possible bid for Imperial Brands sent that stock to the top of the FTSE 100.

Elsewhere, the Thanksgiving storm left nearly a million homes without power and forced Macy's to move its parade to Saturday. Markets are now pricing a near-certain Federal Reserve rate rise in December, and Trump's claim that official GDP figures were fake added a new strain on confidence in US data.

editions.notification: Nvidia's governance now faces a credit warning as the US prepares tariffs on 14 trading partners.
editions.intro:
Nvidia's boardroom drama remains the story markets are watching, but it has moved on from the reinstatement itself. Jensen Huang was reinstated as chief executive on 23 November and the shares surged about 31% that day, adding nearly $1tn in value. The euphoria did not last: Nvidia fell again on Tuesday and was down a further 3.4% on Wednesday, and it remains about 37% below its October peak. Since then S&P Global has put Nvidia's AA rating on watch for a possible downgrade, citing board independence, and four congressional committees and several federal bodies are still probing the affair.

The wider backdrop is a sharp AI-led sell-off that pushed US indexes into correction after Anthropic's record IPO, and spread through Asia. Asian markets bounced on Thursday as investors took the reported US tariff plan on 14 trading partners better than feared. The measures, stemming from a Section 301 investigation, are reportedly unlikely to take effect before February or March, and would add to strains with China ahead of a 10 January expiry of an interim trade deal. Oil is also firm, with Brent near $95 after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery and reported mine strikes in the Strait of Hormuz, while gold fell below $3,500 earlier in the week before steadying.

Elsewhere, Shenzhou-24 carried the first foreign astronaut to Tiangong, and the Chinese anti-graft campaign reached Shanghai party chief Chen Jining. Britain's reservists have been told to be ready for a possible call-up, and the UK and EU published treaties from their post-Brexit reset. Markets are also digesting a US export blacklist of Singapore-based Megaspeed and six other firms, which is rippling into Malaysia's data-centre sector.

Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday, less than two weeks after he resigned, and the shares jumped roughly 30 per cent. The wider AI sell-off remains the bigger story for markets. The S&P 500 and Dow have entered correction after a seventh straight losing session, Asian markets had their steepest slide since 2020, and regulators in China, South Korea and Taiwan have introduced emergency measures. Washington's response has widened the story: the Commerce Department blacklisted Megaspeed and six Southeast Asian firms, Malaysia is working on new licensing curbs, and Alice Huang's alleged links to Chinese intelligence are drawing scrutiny of Lutnick and Bessent.

Elsewhere, the US is reportedly preparing new tariffs on at least 14 trading partners, the Huawei conviction in Brooklyn, and a Chinese anti-graft probe into Shanghai's party chief all add to a crowded news day. Climate talks in Antalya collapsed over fossil fuel language, and a Democratic House majority is set to take shape in Washington.

Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday, less than two weeks after he resigned, and the shares jumped about 30 per cent at the open. Markets are pricing in a quarter-point increase. Europe and the Gulf also dominated the news. Russian cruise missiles crashed in Poland, a Russian cargo ship burned in the Gulf of Finland, and Nato met urgently in Brussels. Iran-linked tensions also continued at sea, with tankers reported to have hit mines in Hormuz, though oil prices fell to near three-month lows.

At home, Andy Burnham's reset deals with the EU drew both praise and fierce opposition, and the Antalya COP31 climate talks collapsed over fossil fuel language. Democrats won their largest House majority since 1992.

editions.notification: Markets in correction after an AI-led rout, even as Anthropic's record IPO trades. Here is what is driving it.
editions.intro:
The AI share sell-off dominates the day. The S&P 500 closed at 6,918.45 on Friday, down 3.59% and in correction, its seventh straight losing session and longest such run since February 2020. The Nasdaq has erased its 2026 gains. Chipmakers led the fall, with Micron, Broadcom, Nvidia and AMD down roughly 12% to 14%. Anthropic's $81bn IPO, the largest ever, has been caught in the rout: it opened at $111.50, closed its debut at $97.17 and fell about 9% on Friday. Asian markets were hit hard, with Taiwan's index recording its steepest weekly drop in decades. Regulators in China, South Korea and Taiwan have responded with emergency steps, including Taiwan's wider short-selling ban, but South Korea's KOSPI still fell 5% on Monday despite pledges of stabilisation funds.

Behind the sell-off are worries about debt-funded AI spending. Reports that Nvidia's $100bn OpenAI deal may not proceed, and reports that Anthropic has around $900bn of spending commitments that could be rated junk, have revived fears of a bubble. Nvidia's leadership is also in turmoil. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive over an affair with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive US intelligence has reportedly linked to Chinese espionage. Bessent now says he would not oppose a return, though Colette Kress remains interim chief executive, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under growing pressure over chip sales to China.

Away from markets, Andy Burnham's UK-EU reset deals on trade, emissions and youth mobility are drawing fire, with student fees still unresolved. Democrats won their largest House majority since the early 1990s. A Lean verification of an Anthropic claim on the Riemann hypothesis adds a notable tech story, though it still needs human review.

Finance.notification: S&P puts Nvidia on downgrade watch as AI stocks swing and the Fed hike bet grows
Finance.summary:
Nvidia's governance is the day's most important market story. S&P Global has put its AA rating on watch for a possible downgrade within 90 days, citing board independence after Jensen Huang resigned and was reinstated within days. The shares are about 38% below their 6 October peak, and the wider AI trade has swung between relief and fear, with Wall Street ending the week higher after a sharp midweek sell-off.

The rate outlook is the other big driver. Futures price a near-certain Federal Reserve rise in December, which has lifted the dollar to a 22-month high around 103.8 and kept Treasury yields elevated. Trump's attack on the official Q3 GDP revision adds a question about the independence of US statistics just as markets lean on that data.

In Asia, shares rebounded after heavy November losses, helped by a softer-than-feared view of new US tariff proposals. Tokyo core inflation at a 16-month high strengthens the case for a Bank of Japan hike, while Nvidia's reported halt of server shipments to four Southeast Asian countries adds supply-chain risk.

World.notification: US Section 301 tariffs on 14-16 trading partners of up to 20% put the China truce at risk
World.summary:
Washington has moved to impose new Section 301 tariffs on at least 14, and by some accounts 16, trading partners, including China, the EU, Japan, Vietnam and India, with rates of up to 20% tied to the trade deals each country has struck. Beijing has said it reserves the right to retaliate, and the proposals, which follow the Supreme Court's February ruling against the earlier tariffs, threaten the fragile US-China truce. Markets are watching Hong Kong, Nike and the S&P 500 for early signs of the hit.

Elsewhere, the UK's Department for Work and Pensions has taken most of its online services offline after a cyber incident, though payments continue. In Europe, S&P has moved France's rating outlook to negative as the economy slipped into a technical recession, and EU leaders failed to agree the 2028-34 budget. The cost of borrowing is the common thread: France's bond yields are at their highest since 2002.

In Asia, China has placed Shanghai party chief Chen Jining under investigation, the fourth Politburo member to fall since 2025, deepening the purge at the top of the Communist Party. Oil prices near $96 a barrel, driven by Middle East attacks on tankers and Saudi energy sites, add to inflation worries.

Tech.notification: OpenAI hits back at Apple, accusing it of pressuring suppliers and monitoring former staff.
Tech.summary:
OpenAI has filed counterclaims against Apple in a California federal court, accusing the iPhone maker of pressuring suppliers not to work on OpenAI devices and of building cases against departing employees. The countersuit turns Apple's trade-secrets lawsuit around. Apple calls it a distraction and notes OpenAI has already been ordered to stop using its confidential information. The dispute centres on OpenAI's hardware push, including a planned device with Jony Ive.

The fight lands as the wider tech market is juggling several pressures. Counterpoint Research says global smartphone shipments fell 9% in the third quarter, with memory prices driving up handset costs, and Apple's share rose to 57%. Separately, the Bank of Korea raised rates amid an AI chip boom, and the Chinese chip trade is under scrutiny after Blackwell servers reportedly turned up in a Shanghai data centre.

Security is the other recurring theme. A reported breach of the US Air Force's Cloud One platform, FIFA's cyber attack and Rackspace shutting its Spot cloud service all point to a rough month for digital defences, while AI-driven fears about encryption are rising at the Bank of England and among cryptographers.

Spanish group Puig has agreed to buy a 75% stake in Artessence, the holding company behind Parfums de Marly and Initio Parfums Privés, from Advent International for €1.2 billion in cash. The deal values the whole company at about $1.9 billion, and the brands' retail sales passed $1 billion in the year to March, up 39%. Completion is expected in the second quarter of 2027.

The acquisition fits Puig's Vision 2032 target of more than €8 billion in sales and its push to lift niche fragrances above €1 billion. Founder Julien Sprecher keeps 25%, with options that could give Puig full ownership over time, and an earn-out tied to performance. Fragrance is proving the strongest growth engine in the sector, and Puig is paying up for it.

Elsewhere, the week's fashion news is mostly about creative change and brand expansion. Alexander McQueen showed its Pre-Fall 2027 collection without a permanent creative director, with an appointment expected early next month. Ferrari opened a Soho store and staged a fall 2027 show in New York, and Fashion Awards honourees were announced for Monday's London ceremony.

Tech.notification: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO, wiping up to $601bn off the chipmaker's value in a day
Tech.summary:
Nvidia's co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as president, chief executive and board member with immediate effect, ending a 33-year run that made the chipmaker worth roughly $4 trillion. The board has named chief financial officer Colette Kress interim chief executive and Harvey Jones as its first independent chair. The exit follows reports of relationships with a woman US intelligence reportedly linked to China's Ministry of State Security and with a direct report, and the shares fell as much as 14% in early trading.

The fallout is spreading across the sector. Democratic senators have asked the administration to preserve records on Nvidia's China chip exports, and reports say the Commerce Department stalled action against Megaspeed, a Singapore firm suspected of routing chips to China. Investors are now focused on Nvidia's third-quarter results on 17 November, the first without Huang, and on whether the AI boom's financing web, which Huang helped build, holds up.

Beyond Nvidia, the sector is under pressure from a broad tech sell-off, AI-linked concerns in US midterm politics, and a heavy pipeline of listings. Anthropic's S-1 filing shows revenue growing very fast, while OpenAI reportedly passed $10bn in quarterly revenue, though with much larger losses.

World.title: Nvidia chief Huang quits amid affair and spy claims
World.notification: Nvidia's Jensen Huang has resigned after 33 years, and the AI trade is asking what comes next.
World.summary:
Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned after 33 years leading the chipmaker, following admissions of affairs, one with a woman US intelligence has determined was a Chinese spy and one with a company executive who reports to him. Nvidia shares fell sharply, and the wider AI trade has been unsettled by fears that a new leader could scale back the company's financing of customers and slow the AI build-out.

The episode also reaches into Washington and Taipei. A Republican senator has called for Huang to go, the House chairman says Huang has agreed to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving, and Taiwan is examining the woman's visits. Chinese AI firms are reportedly rushing to secure Nvidia capacity in case US rules on remote chip access tighten. Analysts will watch governance and export-control moves closely.

Beyond the chip story, the wider news is dominated by the Middle East and Ukraine. Oil rebounded after Trump questioned the need for an Iran deal, while Witkoff and Kushner met Putin, who signalled no compromise. In the UK, Prime Minister Andy Burnham's push for closer EU ties is dividing Westminster ahead of a Brussels summit.

Within luxury, the clearest good news came from Burberry, which swung back to a £54m first-half profit on 6% revenue growth, with wholesale up 17% and the Americas up 12%.

Leadership change is a theme across the sector. Capri has named Estée Lauder veteran Justin Boxford as chief executive from 4 January, ending John Idol's long run, while Tod's has parted ways with creative director Matteo Tamburini. Burberry's Daniel Lee profile and Zimmermann's expansion plans add to the picture of brands leaning on creative direction and new markets.

Demand is the underlying worry. Luxury groups are reportedly turning to the United States as the Chinese growth engine stalls, and Gulf shoppers are cutting back as war-linked inflation bites. Coach and Ralph Lauren are reportedly bucking China's slump, while On Holding posted record sales and margins, helped by tariff refunds.

Tech.title: OpenAI countersues Apple as AI hardware rivalry turns legal
Tech.notification: OpenAI hits back at Apple, accusing it of pressuring suppliers and monitoring former staff.
Tech.summary:
OpenAI has filed counterclaims against Apple in a California federal court, accusing the iPhone maker of pressuring suppliers not to work on OpenAI devices and of building cases against departing employees. The countersuit turns Apple's trade-secrets lawsuit around. Apple calls it a distraction and notes OpenAI has already been ordered to stop using its confidential information. The dispute centres on OpenAI's hardware push, including a planned device with Jony Ive.

The fight lands as the wider tech market is juggling several pressures. Counterpoint Research says global smartphone shipments fell 9% in the third quarter, with memory prices driving up handset costs, and Apple's share rose to 57%. Separately, the Bank of Korea raised rates amid an AI chip boom, and the Chinese chip trade is under scrutiny after Blackwell servers reportedly turned up in a Shanghai data centre.

Security is the other recurring theme. A reported breach of the US Air Force's Cloud One platform, FIFA's cyber attack and Rackspace shutting its Spot cloud service all point to a rough month for digital defences, while AI-driven fears about encryption are rising at the Bank of England and among cryptographers.

Finance.notification: S&P puts Nvidia on downgrade watch as AI stocks swing and the Fed hike bet grows
Finance.summary:
Nvidia's governance is the day's most important market story. S&P Global has put its AA rating on watch for a possible downgrade within 90 days, citing board independence after Jensen Huang resigned and was reinstated within days. The shares are about 38% below their 6 October peak, and the wider AI trade has swung between relief and fear, with Wall Street ending the week higher after a sharp midweek sell-off.

The rate outlook is the other big driver. Futures price a near-certain Federal Reserve rise in December, which has lifted the dollar to a 22-month high around 103.8 and kept Treasury yields elevated. Trump's attack on the official Q3 GDP revision adds a question about the independence of US statistics just as markets lean on that data.

In Asia, shares rebounded after heavy November losses, helped by a softer-than-feared view of new US tariff proposals. Tokyo core inflation at a 16-month high strengthens the case for a Bank of Japan hike, while Nvidia's reported halt of server shipments to four Southeast Asian countries adds supply-chain risk.

World.title: US tariffs on 14-16 partners and China's warning
World.notification: US Section 301 tariffs on 14-16 trading partners of up to 20% put the China truce at risk
World.summary:
Washington has moved to impose new Section 301 tariffs on at least 14, and by some accounts 16, trading partners, including China, the EU, Japan, Vietnam and India, with rates of up to 20% tied to the trade deals each country has struck. Beijing has said it reserves the right to retaliate, and the proposals, which follow the Supreme Court's February ruling against the earlier tariffs, threaten the fragile US-China truce. Markets are watching Hong Kong, Nike and the S&P 500 for early signs of the hit.

Elsewhere, the UK's Department for Work and Pensions has taken most of its online services offline after a cyber incident, though payments continue. In Europe, S&P has moved France's rating outlook to negative as the economy slipped into a technical recession, and EU leaders failed to agree the 2028-34 budget. The cost of borrowing is the common thread: France's bond yields are at their highest since 2002.

In Asia, China has placed Shanghai party chief Chen Jining under investigation, the fourth Politburo member to fall since 2025, deepening the purge at the top of the Communist Party. Oil prices near $96 a barrel, driven by Middle East attacks on tankers and Saudi energy sites, add to inflation worries.

Fashion.title: Puig buys Parfums de Marly and Initio for €1.2bn
Fashion.notification: Puig agrees €1.2bn deal for Parfums de Marly and Initio, brands whose retail sales topped $1bn
Fashion.summary:
Spanish group Puig has agreed to buy a 75% stake in Artessence, the holding company behind Parfums de Marly and Initio Parfums Privés, from Advent International for €1.2 billion in cash. The deal values the whole company at about $1.9 billion, and the brands' retail sales passed $1 billion in the year to March, up 39%. Completion is expected in the second quarter of 2027.

The acquisition fits Puig's Vision 2032 target of more than €8 billion in sales and its push to lift niche fragrances above €1 billion. Founder Julien Sprecher keeps 25%, with options that could give Puig full ownership over time, and an earn-out tied to performance. Fragrance is proving the strongest growth engine in the sector, and Puig is paying up for it.

Elsewhere, the week's fashion news is mostly about creative change and brand expansion. Alexander McQueen showed its Pre-Fall 2027 collection without a permanent creative director, with an appointment expected early next month. Ferrari opened a Soho store and staged a fall 2027 show in New York, and Fashion Awards honourees were announced for Monday's London ceremony.
